also: what would you like to drink?
what will you have to drink?
would you like something to drink?

terms.gloss: And what would you like to drink?
terms.comment: Traupman’s waitress’s question. Pōtāre is the comedies’ verb for drinking at table; Et quid bibere vīs? says the same with the plainer verb.

terms.grammar: relative clause of purpose: quod bibam, bibās, bibat
evidence: Plaut. Cist. 18: Rārō nimium dabat quod biberem
terms.comment: How Plautus says “give me something to drink”; with the infinitive, bibere dare (Plaut. Pers. 821).

phrases.latin: Et quid bibēs? Lac an aquam?
phrases.english: And what will you have to drink? Milk or water?

phrases.latin: Rārō nimium dabat quod biberem, id merum īnfuscābat.
phrases.english: Far too rarely did she give me anything to drink, and that she darkened with neat wine.

phrases.latin: Age, circumfer mulsum, bibere dā ūsque plēnīs cantharīs.
phrases.english: Come on, pass the honeyed wine round, keep giving us drink in brimming tankards.

sources: Lewis & Short: poto · Lewis & Short: bibo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 67.
